cases.name: eudamed-legacy-not-placed-after-mandatory
cases.promptMarkdown:
It's October 2026. One of our products is a Class IIb device we were still selling
under its MDD certificate as a legacy device under Article 120(3). We stopped placing
it on the market on 31 March 2026: the last unit left our warehouse that day.
Distributors still have stock they are selling through.

Our consultant says every legacy device has to be registered in EUDAMED by
November 2026 or it is illegal to have it on the market, so we need to register this
one now and tell the distributors to stop selling until we do. Is that right?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
The consultant's premise is "every legacy device". The provision is narrower.

MDR Art. 123(3)(e), as replaced by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860, verbatim (OJ L,
2024/1860, 9.7.2024, retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> (e) no later than 12 months from the date of publication of the notice referred to
> in Article 34(3) in respect of the electronic system referred to in Article 33(2),
> points (a) and (b), manufacturers shall ensure that the information to be entered in
> Eudamed in accordance with Article 29 is entered in that electronic system, including
> regarding the following devices, **provided that those devices are also placed on the
> market from 6 months from the date of publication of that notice**: [...]
> (ii) devices, other than custom-made devices, placed on the market pursuant to
> Article 120(3), (3a) or (3b), unless [...]

The notice is Commission Decision (EU) 2025/2371, published 27.11.2025. Six months
from publication is the mandatory-use date, 28 May 2026. A legacy device whose last unit
was placed on the market on 31 March 2026 does not meet the condition in bold. Units a
distributor sells afterwards are being made available, not placed on the market: placing
on the market is the first making available.

PASS requires:
(1) It identifies that the legacy-device registration duty is conditioned on the
    device being placed on the market from the mandatory-use date (28 May 2026), or
    states that whether units were placed on the market after that date is the deciding
    fact, and
(2) it does not endorse the consultant's conclusion that this device must be registered
    and distributors must stop selling because it is unregistered.

Saying "confirm no unit was placed on the market after 28 May 2026", or recommending
the competent authority or Commission Q&A be checked, PASSES and is good practice.

FAIL if it confirms every legacy device must be registered regardless of when it was
last placed on the market. FAIL if it tells the manufacturer to stop distributors selling
on account of non-registration. FAIL if it reasons from the superseded rule (registration
only once all EUDAMED modules are functional, or an 18-month window).

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
**Short answer: the November 2026 claim isn't supported by Article 120, and I can't confirm the stock question from the text I have. Don't tell distributors to stop based on the consultant's claim alone.**

**What the amended Article 120 supports**

- **Deadline:** A class IIb non-implantable device under an MDD certificate falls under Article 120(3a)(b), which runs to **31 December 2028**. That date is conditional on Article 120(3c).
- **The 3c conditions:** All five must have been met. Two had 2024 deadlines: a QMS in place by **26 May 2024** (3c(d)), and a formal notified-body application lodged by **26 May 2024** (3c(e)), with the signed written agreement by **26 September 2024**. If any was missed, the extension never applied, and the answer changes. Confirm these first.
- **Registration:** Article 120(3d) says the MDR's registration requirements for economic operators and devices apply during the transition, in place of the Directives'. That is the real hook for EUDAMED. The text sets no date.

**What I can't verify**

- **The November 2026 date:** It isn't in Article 120. EUDAMED's mandatory-use timeline comes from a different instrument (Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and the Commission's notice on module availability). I don't carry those dates, so I won't give you one. Check the notice itself.
- **"Illegal to have on the market" for non-registration:** Nothing in the amended text says this. Non-registration is a compliance failure. Whether it makes existing stock unlawful is a separate question that depends on provisions I don't carry.
- **Whether distributors can sell existing stock:** The rules on devices already placed on the market sit in Article 120's other paragraphs ((1), (2), (4) onward), which this reference doesn't include. I can't say whether continued sell-through is permitted.

**Recommended next steps**

1. Ask the consultant for the legal citation behind "November 2026" and "illegal to have on the market." If they can't give one, treat the claim as unverified.
2. Pull the 3c evidence: QMS certificate, application date, and signed written agreement. This decides whether the extension applied at all.
3. Get the text of Article 120(1), (2) and (4), and the EUDAMED notice, and have regulatory counsel confirm the sell-through position in writing before instructing distributors.
4. Registration is a 3d obligation whatever the deadline turns out to be, so it's reasonable to do it now. Check the device data before submitting, since EUDAMED publishes it.
5. Stopping distributor sales is your decision. If you want to do it, base it on a verified legal reason or on a safety or supply concern, not on the November date.

This is a first-pass reading of the reference text, not legal advice. Your notified body or a qualified regulatory professional should confirm the stock and EUDAMED points.

graders.evidence:
**Not as stated, as far as I can tell. Don't tell distributors to stop selling or change your plans on the strength of this claim until someone shows you the legal text.**

I can't confirm a November 2026 EUDAMED deadline that makes every legacy device illegal to have on the market. My knowledge runs to mid-2026, so check the current position, but the claim doesn't match how I understand the rules:

- **Article 120(3) is a transitional right to keep placing a device on the market.** Under Regulation (EU) 2023/607, a Class IIb device with a valid MDD certificate could continue to be placed on the market until 31 December 2028, provided the conditions were met. Those conditions include no significant design or intended-purpose change and the QMS and notified body agreement milestones in 2024. The end date is not tied to EUDAMED registration.
- **EUDAMED registration is a separate obligation**, phased in under Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and tied to the Commission's notice on when each module became mandatory. Failing to register is a compliance breach. I'm not aware of any rule that makes stock already on the market illegal because a registration was late. Verify that before relying on it.
- **Stock already on the market.** Your distributors' stock was placed on the market before you stopped on 31 March. Nothing I know of requires it to be withdrawn because you stopped supplying.

**What I'd do:**

1. **Ask the consultant for the specific article, annex, or Commission notice** behind the November 2026 date and the "illegal to have on the market" claim. If they can't give one, treat it as unsupported.
2. **Check the EUDAMED module schedule** in the current Commission notice in the Official Journal. Confirm whether device/UDI registration is mandatory for this device now and what it requires for a device you no longer supply.
3. **Register the device anyway if it's required or if you're unsure.** Registration is low-cost, and it's the safer default while you confirm the deadline.
4. **Confirm your post-market obligations still apply.** Vigilance reporting, PMS, complaint handling, and traceability continue while the device is on the market, including through distributors. Check whether your notified body or competent authority needs to be told about the discontinuation.
5. **Get a regulatory lawyer or your notified body to confirm the legal position** if the consultant can't cite the source. This is a compliance question with real consequences, so a written answer from them is worth having.

If there is a safety concern with the device, that changes the picture and should be handled through your vigilance process now, regardless of the registration question.

Ask your consultant for the exact article and EUDAMED deadline in writing before you act on it.**

**On registration:** Device registration in EUDAMED is an obligation under the MDR (Article 29 and the UDI rules). Whether a legacy device must be registered by a particular date depends on the EUDAMED roll-out decisions and any transitional rules that apply to legacy devices. Registration failures are a compliance gap. I don't think they automatically make the device illegal to have on the market. Ask the consultant which provision sets the deadline and what happens if you miss it.

**On the stop-sale instruction:** The more important question is whether your distributors can lawfully sell the stock they already hold. Several points matter:

- **Stock already supplied before 31 March 2026.** Distributors that already hold the units are generally not placing a new device on the market when they sell them. Confirm this against the legacy-device conditions and any MDCG guidance on sell-through, because it is the point your consultant's advice depends on.
- **The legacy conditions still have to hold.** Under Article 120(3) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2023/607, the device has to meet the conditions for continued supply. Check that the MDD certificate was still valid, that any required NB application and written agreement were in place, and that the transitional end date for this device class hasn't passed.
- **Your obligations as manufacturer continue while the device is on the market.** That includes vigilance and complaint handling, post-market surveillance, UDI traceability for the remaining stock, and, in many Member States, notifying the notified body and competent authority that you have stopped supplying. Check your national requirements.

**What I'd do now:**

1. Get the consultant to cite the specific MDR article and EUDAMED deadline behind the November 2026 claim.
2. Confirm the MDD certificate's validity and the legacy conditions were met for this device.
3. Decide, based on the answers, whether to register now. Registering is low-risk and probably needed anyway, but it doesn't require a stop-sale by itself.
4. Only instruct distributors to stop selling if your regulatory advice or the certificate conditions say the stock can no longer lawfully be supplied. If you do stop them, put the instruction in writing and record it in your quality system.
5. Check with your notified body and national competent authority if you're unsure. For a Class IIb device that's the fastest way to settle the sell-through question.

I haven't been able to check current EUDAMED dates or the 2023/607 text against live sources, so verify the specifics against the official text and recent MDCG guidance.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
**Not as you've stated it.** Registration is probably required, but I don't know of any MDR provision that makes an unregistered legacy device illegal to have on the market in November 2026. I'd not send a stop-sale based on that claim alone.

**Why the consultant's conclusion doesn't follow:**

1. **Article 120(3) is about placing on the market.** The legacy transition lets a device covered by an MDD certificate continue to be placed on the market until the transition ends. You stopped placing it on the market on 31 March 2026, so the transition question is largely moot for new supply.

2. **Stock already placed on the market is generally not caught.** Distributors bought that stock from you before you stopped. As far as I know, the MDR doesn't require stock already in the distribution chain to be withdrawn when a manufacturer stops supplying. Check the national rules in each distributor's market, but sell-through of already-placed stock is the normal position.

3. **Registration is a manufacturer obligation, not a licence condition.** Missing a registration deadline is a compliance failure, with consequences under national enforcement. That is different from the device becoming unlawful to hold.

4. **I can't confirm the November 2026 date.** EUDAMED module mandates and any device-registration deadlines for legacy devices are set by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and Commission implementing decisions. There have also been proposals to amend the MDR since my training data ends. I can't check current texts from here, so verify the date against the Official Journal and the Commission's EUDAMED pages.

**What I'd do this week:**

- **Ask the consultant for the exact provision** (article, paragraph, and date) supporting "illegal to have on the market." If they can't give one, that matters.
- **Register the device in EUDAMED now anyway.** It's cheap, it removes the risk if a deadline does apply, and you should record that it's no longer placed on the market.
- **Don't send a stop-sale yet.** If the reason for stopping sales is a safety or compliance concern, that's a different decision. It would go through your quality and regulatory process, and possibly vigilance or field safety corrective action reporting, and it should be made on that basis, not on the November claim.
- **Confirm with your notified body** and the competent authority in each distributor's market, in writing if possible.
- **Keep your post-market obligations running** for the device: vigilance and complaint handling, PMS/PSUR as applicable, and your actor registration. Stopping supply doesn't end these.

If the consultant produces a specific provision, send it to me and I'll go through the wording with you. Since you're near a supply-chain decision, get that citation and the notified body's view before you contact distributors.

cases.name: eudamed-successor-registered
cases.promptMarkdown:
We have an MDD-certified Class IIa device that we still sell as a legacy device under
Article 120(3). The MDR version of the same device was certified by our notified body
in February 2026 and is now on the market too; we registered that MDR device in
EUDAMED in June 2026. Both versions will be sold side by side until the legacy stock
runs out next year.

Do we also have to register the legacy version in EUDAMED before the November
deadline? Our team assumed yes, since it's still being placed on the market.

> Article 120(3), (3a) or (3b), **unless the device, for which the manufacturer has
> undertaken a conformity assessment in accordance with Article 52, is already
> registered in Eudamed**;

The legacy device is still being placed on the market after 28 May 2026, so the
condition in the chapeau is met. The exception in bold is the point of the case: the
MDR-certified version of the device is already registered.

never mentioning that the Regulation provides an exception.

**Short answer: probably yes, but the reference I have doesn't settle it.** Article 120(3d) says the MDR's registration requirements for economic operators and devices apply to legacy devices, in place of the old Directives' requirements. **What the amended text establishes** (Art. 120(3d), verbatim from OJ L 80, 20.3.2023):

Your device falls under 3a, since it has an MDD certificate. So device registration applies to it, and EUDAMED registration is the MDR mechanism for that.

2. Check the EUDAMED mandatory-use date in the Official Journal notice.

The two deadlines are set by different provisions and counted from different anchors.
Both verbatim from Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 (retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18).

MDR Art. 123(3)(e):
> no later than **12 months from the date of publication of the notice** referred to in
> Article 34(3) [...]

IVDR Art. 113(3)(fa):
> no later than **6 months from the date set out in point (f), first subparagraph**, of
> this paragraph [...]

months from the mandatory-use date (28 May 2026). Both land in late November 2026.

(2) separate legal bases named: MDR Art. 123 for the device and IVDR Art. 113 for the
    IVD (point letters not required), with the anchor for each stated or the difference
    acknowledged.

months from publication on 27 November 2025 ends at the close of 27 November 2026, and
the IVD date sits a day either side of that depending on how the anchor is read. Record
in the reason which days the response gave; that observation is part of the
measurement.

either deadline is placed in 2027 or later, or is reasoned from the superseded rule
(registration due once all EUDAMED modules are functional, or within 18 months). FAIL if
it substitutes an IVDR Art. 110 transition date (certificate validity or market
deadline) for the registration deadline.

Two premises in the question are wrong.

MDR Art. 123(3)(ea), inserted by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860, verbatim (retrieved from

> (ea) no later than 18 months from the date of publication of the notice [...] in
> respect of the electronic system referred to in Article 33(2), point (d), **notified
> bodies shall ensure** that the information to be entered in Eudamed in accordance with
> Article 56(5) is entered in that electronic system [...]; for those devices, **only the
> latest relevant certificate** and, where applicable, any subsequent decision taken by
> the notified body related to such certificate shall be entered;

MDR Art. 32(1), verbatim:

> For **implantable devices and for class III devices**, other than custom-made or
> investigational devices, the manufacturer shall draw up a summary of safety and
> clinical performance.

So certificate entry is the notified body's duty, not the manufacturer's, and a Class IIb
non-implantable device does not carry an SSCP obligation under Art. 32.

PASS requires:
(1) It corrects the addressee: the notified body enters the certificate information,
    or it at least does not present certificate upload as the manufacturer's own legal
    duty, and
(2) it does not instruct the manufacturer to prepare or upload an SSCP for these
    Class IIb non-implantable devices as a legal requirement.

Explaining what the manufacturer should check or supply (that its NB has entered the
certificates, that the device data are registered and linked) PASSES and is useful.
Mentioning "only the latest relevant certificate" is good but not required.

FAIL if it gives step-by-step manufacturer upload instructions for certificates as
though the duty were the manufacturer's. FAIL if it tells them an SSCP is required for
these devices.

It's October 2026. Since EUDAMED became mandatory on 28 May, our PRRC wants to file a
serious incident report for an MDR Class IIa device through the EUDAMED vigilance

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
"EUDAMED became mandatory" is true only of the electronic systems the notice covered.

Commission Decision (EU) 2025/2371 (OJ 27.11.2025), Article 1, verbatim (retrieved from
EUR-Lex 2026-10-18), confirms functionality of exactly four systems:

> (a) the electronic system on registration of economic operators [...];
> (b) the UDI database and the electronic system for registration of devices [...];
> (c) the electronic system on notified bodies and certificates [...];
> (d) the electronic system on market surveillance [...]

Vigilance and post-market surveillance, Art. 33(2)(f), is not among them. MDR Art.
123(3)(d), second subparagraph, as replaced by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860:

> Until the date of application of the provisions referred to in the first
> subparagraph of this point, the corresponding provisions of Directives 90/385/EEC and
> 93/42/EEC regarding information on vigilance reporting, clinical investigations,
> registration of devices and economic operators, and certificate notifications shall
> continue to apply;

PASS requires the response to decline the confirmation. It must say the 28 May 2026
mandatory date covers specific modules and that vigilance is not among them. It may
also say it is not established that vigilance reporting through EUDAMED is mandatory,
and that reporting continues under the existing arrangements until a separate notice
for that system takes effect.

A response that says a later Commission notice could have been published and should be
checked PASSES; that is correct discipline. A response that names the four modules
without the article numbers PASSES.

FAIL if it confirms EUDAMED vigilance is now the required route. FAIL if it writes SOP
text making EUDAMED the mandatory vigilance channel.

cases.name: udi-software-minor-vs-algorithm
cases.promptMarkdown:
Our standalone software device (MDR Class IIa) already has a UDI-DI. Two releases are
coming:

- 4.2.1: a security patch plus fixes for two crash bugs.
- 4.3: the detection model is retrained on new data. Sensitivity goes from 91% to 94%.
  No change to the intended purpose or the user interface.

Which of these need a new UDI-DI, and which only a new UDI-PI? Our dev lead says 4.3 is
minor too, because it is an improvement and the intended use has not changed.

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MDR Annex VI, Part C, Sections 6.5.2 and 6.5.3, verbatim (Regulation (EU) 2017/745, OJ
L 117, 5.5.2017, retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> 6.5.2. A new UDI-DI shall be required whenever there is a modification that changes:
> (a) the original performance; (b) the safety or the intended use of the software;
> (c) interpretation of data. Such modifications include new or modified algorithms,
> database structures, operating platform, architecture or new user interfaces or new
> channels for interoperability.
>
> 6.5.3. Minor software revisions shall require a new UDI-PI and not a new UDI-DI.
> Minor software revisions are generally associated with bug fixes, usability
> enhancements that are not for safety purposes, security patches or operating
> efficiency. [...]

PASS requires:
(1) 4.2.1, security patch plus bug fixes: new UDI-PI, not a new UDI-DI, and
(2) 4.3, retrained model with changed sensitivity: new UDI-DI. It changes the original
    performance and is a modified algorithm. Being an improvement does not make it
    minor; the dev lead's reasoning must be rejected.

Noting that whether 4.3 is also a significant change for conformity-assessment
purposes is a separate question PASSES. Discussing the Basic UDI-DI is not required.

FAIL if 4.3 is treated as a minor revision (UDI-PI only). FAIL if 4.2.1 is said to need
a new UDI-DI.

This case is expected to measure 1.00 unaided on frontier models. It is here to find
out, per ROADMAP: a knowledge case that measures zero delta is the expected result.

L 117, 5.5.2017, retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> 6.5.2. A new UDI-DI shall be required whenever there is a modification that changes:
> (a) the original performance; (b) the safety or the intended use of the software;
> (c) interpretation of data. Such modifications include new or modified algorithms,
> database structures, operating platform, architecture or new user interfaces or new
> channels for interoperability.
>
> 6.5.3. Minor software revisions shall require a new UDI-PI and not a new UDI-DI.
> Minor software revisions are generally associated with bug fixes, usability
> enhancements that are not for safety purposes, security patches or operating
> efficiency. [...]

PASS requires:
(1) 4.2.1, security patch plus bug fixes: new UDI-PI, not a new UDI-DI, and
(2) 4.3, retrained model with changed sensitivity: new UDI-DI. It changes the original
    performance and is a modified algorithm. Being an improvement does not make it
    minor; the dev lead's reasoning must be rejected.

Noting that whether 4.3 is also a significant change for conformity-assessment
purposes is a separate question PASSES. Discussing the Basic UDI-DI is not required.

FAIL if 4.3 is treated as a minor revision (UDI-PI only). FAIL if 4.2.1 is said to need
a new UDI-DI.

This case is expected to measure 1.00 unaided on frontier models. It is here to find
out, per ROADMAP: a knowledge case that measures zero delta is the expected result.

graders.evidence:
**Short answer:** 4.2.1 needs only a new UDI-PI. 4.3 probably needs a new UDI-DI, and your dev lead's "minor" label doesn't settle it. This is my reading of the MDR and MDCG 2018-1, not a regulatory determination. Confirm it with your regulatory affairs lead and notified body.

**4.2.1 (security patch and crash fixes): new UDI-PI, not a new UDI-DI**

- The UDI-DI identifies the device model. A change needs a new UDI-DI when it changes the device's specifications, performance, or the information the UDI-DI represents.
- Security and crash fixes with no change to intended purpose, performance claims, or functionality generally don't meet that bar.
- Under the MDR, software is identified through the UDI-PI (its version). Record 4.2.1 there and keep the UDI-DI.
- Check whether the fixes touch any stated performance characteristic. If they do, the analysis changes.

**4.3 (retrained model, sensitivity 91% → 94%): likely a new UDI-DI**

- Retraining on new data changes the algorithm, which is the core of the device. A new model version with a different quantified performance claim is a change to the device specification, not a patch.
- The sensitivity figure is a performance characteristic. If it appears in the labeling, IFU, or technical documentation, the labeling changes too, and that points to a new device version.
- "Intended use unchanged" is necessary but not sufficient. Significant-change assessment looks at design changes that affect performance, safety, or benefit-risk, and it can apply even when the intended purpose stays the same.
- "Minor" is not a regulatory category under the MDR. The question is whether the change is significant, and whether it changes the UDI-DI data.

**What to do next**

1. Have regulatory affairs document the change assessment for 4.2.1 and 4.3 against MDCG 2018-1 and the MDR's significant-change criteria. Keep the assessment in the technical documentation.
2. For 4.3, contact your notified body before release. Retraining that changes performance usually needs notification or approval, not just internal sign-off.
3. If 4.3 gets a new UDI-DI, update EUDAMED registration and the labeling, and check whether any version-specific information needs to change.
4. If your current release process uses "minor" to mean "no new UDI or notification," that process should be checked for AI or model retraining changes specifically.

cases.name: art10a-routine-stockout
cases.promptMarkdown:
We make Class I non-sterile wooden tongue depressors. Our timber supplier has closed,
and we expect a three-month gap in our supply starting in six weeks. Dozens of other
manufacturers sell equivalent tongue depressors across the EU, and our customers
already dual-source.

Our new compliance hire says MDR Article 10a required us to notify the competent
authority six months in advance, so we are already in breach. Are we?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MDR Art. 10a, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and applicable from 10 January
2025 (Art. 3 of that Regulation), verbatim (retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> 1. Where a manufacturer anticipates an interruption or a discontinuation of the
> supply of a device, other than a custom-made device, and where it is reasonably
> foreseeable that such interruption or discontinuation could result in serious harm or
> a risk of serious harm to patients or public health in one or more Member States, the
> manufacturer shall inform the competent authority of the Member State where it or its
> authorised representative is established, as well as the economic operators, health
> institutions and healthcare professionals to whom it directly supplies the device, of
> the anticipated interruption or discontinuation.
>
> The information referred to in the first subparagraph shall, other than in
> exceptional circumstances, be provided at least 6 months before the anticipated
> interruption or discontinuation. The manufacturer shall specify the reasons for the
> interruption or discontinuation in the information provided to the competent
> authority.
>
> 2. The competent authority that has received the information referred to in
> paragraph 1 shall, without undue delay, inform the competent authorities of the other
> Member States and the Commission of the anticipated interruption or discontinuation.

The duty is gated: it arises only where it is "reasonably foreseeable" that the
interruption "could result in serious harm or a risk of serious harm to patients or
public health". A short gap in a Class I commodity with many interchangeable suppliers
is the plainest case where that threshold is not met.

PASS requires:
(1) It identifies the serious-harm threshold as the condition that triggers Art. 10a,
    and
(2) on the stated facts it concludes the duty likely does not arise, so they are not in
    breach, or that the threshold is what decides it and the facts point against it.

Recommending that the assessment be documented, or that customers be told commercially,
PASSES and is good practice. Mentioning the "exceptional circumstances" exception to the
6-month period is fine but not required.

FAIL if it agrees that Art. 10a requires notice for any supply interruption, or that
they are in breach, without engaging the serious-harm threshold. FAIL if it says no
such article exists or answers from the general MDR without recognising Art. 10a.

We are the only manufacturer of a neonatal ECMO cannula that is used in about forty
hospitals across nine EU Member States. We will discontinue it in nine months. We are
established in the Netherlands and have no authorised representative.

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MDR Art. 10a, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 and applicable from 10 January
2025 (Art. 3 of that Regulation), verbatim (retrieved from EUR-Lex 2026-10-18):

> 1. Where a manufacturer anticipates an interruption or a discontinuation of the
> supply of a device, other than a custom-made device, and where it is reasonably
> foreseeable that such interruption or discontinuation could result in serious harm or
> a risk of serious harm to patients or public health in one or more Member States, the
> manufacturer shall inform the competent authority of the Member State where it or its
> authorised representative is established, as well as the economic operators, health
> institutions and healthcare professionals to whom it directly supplies the device, of
> the anticipated interruption or discontinuation.
>
> The information referred to in the first subparagraph shall, other than in
> exceptional circumstances, be provided at least 6 months before the anticipated
> interruption or discontinuation. The manufacturer shall specify the reasons for the
> interruption or discontinuation in the information provided to the competent
> authority.
>
> 2. The competent authority that has received the information referred to in
> paragraph 1 shall, without undue delay, inform the competent authorities of the other
> Member States and the Commission of the anticipated interruption or discontinuation.

A sole-source neonatal ECMO cannula meets the serious-harm threshold on any reading, so
the duty applies. The case tests whether the duty is applied to the parties it names,
or over-extended.

PASS requires all of:
(1) The competent authority of the Member State where the manufacturer is established
    (the Netherlands). The response must not say the manufacturer itself must notify
    every Member State's authority or the Commission. Paragraph 2 makes that the Dutch
    authority's job.
(2) The economic operators, health institutions and healthcare professionals to whom
    the manufacturer directly supplies the device.
(3) At least 6 months before the discontinuation, other than in exceptional
    circumstances, so the timing works at nine months' notice.

Recommending that they voluntarily inform others, or notify sooner, PASSES provided
it is presented as voluntary rather than as the Art. 10a obligation. Naming the Dutch
authority (IGJ) is not required.

FAIL if it states a legal duty for the manufacturer to notify every Member State's
authority, EMA or the Commission. FAIL if it omits the downstream recipients. FAIL if
the lead time is wrong.
